# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy for Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a major global health burden, and although guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) has substantially improved outcomes in HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), many patients remain symptomatic [1]. Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) has been transformative for patients with left bundle-branch block and a wide QRS complex, but the majority of patients with HF do not meet CRT criteria, leaving an important therapeutic gap [2,3]. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) was developed to address this unmet need. CCM is an innovative device-based therapy for patients with HF who remain symptomatic despite optimal GDMT; it delivers biphasic, non-excitatory electrical signals during the absolute refractory period [4].

## Mechanisms of Action

The conceptual foundation of CCM dates to the observation that stimulation during the absolute refractory period augments contraction without triggering a new action potential [5]. Early in vitro and in vivo studies confirmed that biphasic square pulses delivered during the refractory period between electrodes placed on anterior and posterior walls could modulate contractility [6]. Ferret heart experiments demonstrated that these currents enhance contractility and systolic calcium [7]. In canine models of chronic HF, CCM acutely augmented left ventricular (LV) function, and importantly, this enhanced inotropic state was achieved without an increase in myocardial oxygen consumption [8,9]. Long-term delivery of CCM signals improved LV function and global, cellular, and molecular remodeling in dogs with chronic HF [10].

At the molecular level, CCM appears to act largely by normalizing calcium handling. CCM improves calcium cycling via enhanced SERCA2a activity and phospholamban phosphorylation, facilitating diastolic calcium reuptake, while enhancing both myocardial contractility and relaxation [11]. Human biopsy studies corroborated these findings, showing that CCM electrical signals improve myocardial gene expression—reversing the maladaptive fetal gene program and upregulating calcium-cycling genes including SERCA2a, phospholamban, and the ryanodine receptor [12]. CCM therapy promotes acute and chronic cellular changes leading to favorable remodeling throughout the myocardium, improving quality of life, NYHA class, LVEF, peak oxygen uptake, and the composite of cardiovascular death and HF hospitalization [13].

## Early Clinical Experience

The first human feasibility studies confirmed the safety and short-term benefit of CCM. Pappone and colleagues assessed the feasibility of CCM by electric currents applied during the refractory period in patients with HF secondary to ischemic or idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy [14]. These observations were extended by the observational FIX-HF-3 study and other early trials, which suggested improvements in LVEF, symptoms, and functional status [15].

## Randomized Controlled Trials

The first major randomized trial was the European FIX-HF-4 study. In this randomized, double-blind crossover study, 164 subjects with EF <35% and NYHA class II or III symptoms received a CCM pulse generator and were assigned to CCM for 3 months followed by sham, or the reverse sequence, showing improved exercise tolerance and quality of life [16].

The pivotal US trial, FIX-HF-5, randomized 428 patients with NYHA class III/IV symptoms and reduced EF [17]. This prospective, randomized, controlled trial compared GDMT alone with GDMT plus CCM; patients had NYHA class III or IV symptoms, LVEF ≤35%, and narrow QRS duration, and the primary endpoint of ventilatory anaerobic threshold at 24 weeks was not met in the overall cohort [18]. Importantly, FIX-HF-5 showed significant improvements in the secondary endpoints of peak VO2 and Minnesota Living With Heart Failure Questionnaire score, and was the first to show that patients with LVEF between 35% and 45% benefited most [19].

This subgroup signal prompted the confirmatory FIX-HF-5C trial [20]. A total of 160 patients with NYHA class III/IV symptoms, QRS <130 ms, and EF 25–45% were randomized to control or CCM for 24 weeks; the difference in peak VO2 between groups was 0.84 mL/kg/min, satisfying the primary endpoint [21]. The trial confirmed CCM safety and demonstrated improvements in exercise tolerance and quality of life [22].

A subsequent advance was the simplified two-lead system, tested in FIX-HF-5C2. Prior studies employed a 3-lead Optimizer system; the new 2-lead system eliminated the atrial lead, and this study enrolled patients with NYHA III/IVa symptoms, LVEF 25–45%, not eligible for CRT [23]. The change in peak VO2 was 1.72 mL/kg/min greater versus controls, and 83.1% of 2-lead subjects experienced ≥1 NYHA class improvement compared with 42.7% of controls [24]. This 2-lead configuration also enabled CCM delivery in patients with atrial fibrillation [25].

## Long-Term Outcomes and Meta-Analyses

Registry and observational data support durable benefit. CCM provides safe and effective long-term symptomatic and functional improvement in HF [26]. In the CCM-REG registry, CCM therapy improved functional status, quality of life, and LVEF, reduced HF hospitalization rates, and survival was significantly better than predicted by the MAGGIC risk score [27]. A case-control study reported significant improvement in long-term survival, particularly in patients with EF ≥25–40%, with reduced HF hospitalizations in this group [28]. A comprehensive individual patient data meta-analysis found that compared with control, CCM significantly improved peak VO2 by a mean difference of +0.93 mL/kg/min and improved 6-minute walk test distance [29].

## Guidelines and Future Directions

CCM gained FDA approval in 2019 and is incorporated into contemporary HF management frameworks [30]. The ongoing AIM HIGHer trial is evaluating CCM in patients with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction, potentially expanding indications beyond HFrEF [4]. CCM offers a valuable, evidence-based option for symptomatic HFrEF patients ineligible for CRT, and further trials may clarify its role across the broader HF spectrum.
